claim: PIKfyve inhibition with apilimod delayed wound healing by 45% compared to vehicle control in cultured cells.
source: In cultured cells, compared to vehicle control, PIKfyve inhibition with apilimod and YM201636 delayed wound healing by 45% and 40%, respectively (Figure 1A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from wound healing assays shown in Figure 1A-B, where quantification demonstrates the percentage of wound closure.

claim: PIKfyve inhibition with YM201636 delayed wound healing by 40% compared to vehicle control in cultured cells.
source: In cultured cells, compared to vehicle control, PIKfyve inhibition with apilimod and YM201636 delayed wound healing by 45% and 40%, respectively (Figure 1A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from wound healing assays shown in Figure 1A-B, where quantification demonstrates the percentage of wound closure.

claim: Inhibition of PIKfyve did not significantly affect cell viability.
source: Importantly, inhibition of PIKfyve did not significantly affect cell viability or proliferation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), indicating that the delay in wound healing reflects a decrease in the ability of the cells to migrate.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from cell viability assays shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Inhibition of PIKfyve did not significantly affect cell proliferation.
source: Importantly, inhibition of PIKfyve did not significantly affect cell viability or proliferation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), indicating that the delay in wound healing reflects a decrease in the ability of the cells to migrate.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from cell proliferation assays shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The delay in wound healing following PIKfyve inhibition reflects a decrease in the ability of cells to migrate.
source: Importantly, inhibition of PIKfyve did not significantly affect cell viability or proliferation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), indicating that the delay in wound healing reflects a decrease in the ability of the cells to migrate.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that PIKfyve inhibition delays wound healing without affecting viability or proliferation, suggesting migration is the affected process.

claim: Inhibition of PIKfyve with YM201636 impaired wound closure by 21% in primary neonatal cardiac fibroblasts compared to DMSO-treated cells.
source: Inhibition of PIKfyve with YM201636 impaired wound closure by 21% as compared to DMSO-treated cardiac fibroblasts (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A-B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from wound healing assays in primary cardiac fibroblasts shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A-B.

claim: Similar results to YM201636 were observed with apilimod in primary neonatal cardiac fibroblasts.
source: Similar results were observed with apilimod (Cinato et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study by Cinato et al., 2021.

claim: PIKfyveβ-geo/β-geo fibroblasts showed a 30% reduction in wound healing compared to wild-type fibroblasts.
source: PIKfyveβ-geo/β-geo fibroblasts showed strong defects in cell migration and exhibited a 30% reduction in wound healing compared to wild-type fibroblasts (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C-D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from wound healing assays using fibroblasts from hypomorphic PIKfyve mice shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C-D.

claim: Inhibition of PIKfyve for 1 hr reduced cell spreading by 22% compared to DMSO-treated control cells.
source: We found that inhibition of PIKfyve for 1 hr reduced cell spreading by 22% as compared to DMSO-treated control cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E-F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from cell spreading assays shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2E-F.

claim: Induction of PIKfyve-KYA caused a significant increase in wound healing by approximately 20%.
source: Induction of PIKfyve-KYA caused a significant increase in wound healing, by approximately 20%, whereas induction of wild-type PIKfyve resulted in a similar degree of cell migration to that observed in control cells (Figure 1C–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from wound healing assays using inducible PIKfyve-KYA cell lines shown in Figure 1C-D.

claim: Induction of wild-type PIKfyve resulted in a similar degree of cell migration to that observed in control cells.
source: Induction of PIKfyve-KYA caused a significant increase in wound healing, by approximately 20%, whereas induction of wild-type PIKfyve resulted in a similar degree of cell migration to that observed in control cells (Figure 1C–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from wound healing assays using inducible wild-type PIKfyve cell lines shown in Figure 1C-D.

claim: PIKfyve activity directly impacts cell migration.
source: Together, these results suggest that PIKfyve activity directly impacts cell migration.
evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple experimental results showing that both inhibition and activation of PIKfyve affect cell migration.

claim: Apilimod treatment for 1 hr resulted in 21% less surface-exposed β1-integrin compared to DMSO-treated cells using immunofluorescence.
source: Notably, using immunofluorescence or flow cytometry, which allowed us to count many more cells, we found that when compared with DMSO-treated cells, apilimod treatment for 1 hr resulted in 21% and 18% less surface-exposed β1-integrin, respectively (Figure 1E–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from immunofluorescence measurements shown in Figure 1E-F.

claim: Apilimod treatment for 1 hr resulted in 18% less surface-exposed β1-integrin compared to DMSO-treated cells using flow cytometry.
source: Notably, using immunofluorescence or flow cytometry, which allowed us to count many more cells, we found that when compared with DMSO-treated cells, apilimod treatment for 1 hr resulted in 21% and 18% less surface-exposed β1-integrin, respectively (Figure 1E–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from flow cytometry measurements shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Depletion of PIKfyve leads to a 21% decrease in surface levels of β1-integrin compared to control siRNA-treated cells.
source: Compared to control siRNA-treated cells, depletion of PIKfyve leads to a decrease in surface levels of β1-integrin by 21%.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from siRNA knockdown experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Simultaneous expression of siRNA-resistant PIKfyve in siRNA-treated cells rescued integrin levels and increased them to 21% above the levels in cells treated with control siRNA alone.
source: Importantly, simultaneous expression of siRNA-resistant PIKfyve in siRNA-treated cells rescued integrin levels and furthermore increased them to 21% above the levels in cells treated with control siRNA alone (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B-C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from rescue experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B-C.

claim: Transient expression of wild-type PIKfyve resulted in a 60% increase in β1-integrin on the cell surface compared to untransfected control cells.
source: We transiently expressed wild-type PIKfyve and PIKfyve-KYA in HeLa cells, and observed a 60% and 107% increase, respectively, in β1-integrin on the cell surface as compared to untransfected control cells (Figure 1H–I).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from transient transfection experiments shown in Figure 1H-I.

claim: Transient expression of PIKfyve-KYA resulted in a 107% increase in β1-integrin on the cell surface compared to untransfected control cells.
source: We transiently expressed wild-type PIKfyve and PIKfyve-KYA in HeLa cells, and observed a 60% and 107% increase, respectively, in β1-integrin on the cell surface as compared to untransfected control cells (Figure 1H–I).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from transient transfection experiments shown in Figure 1H-I.

claim: PIKfyve activity regulates cell migration in part by regulating surface levels of β1-integrin.
source: These findings suggest that PIKfyve activity regulates cell migration in part by regulating surface levels of β1-integrin.
evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple experimental results showing that PIKfyve activity correlates with β1-integrin surface levels and cell migration.

claim: Fibroblasts from a hypomorphic PIKfyveβ-geo/β-geo mouse mutant, which expresses 10% of wild-type levels of PIKfyve, had approximately half of the normal levels of PI3,5P2 and PI5P.
source: In an earlier study we found that fibroblasts from a hypomorphic PIKfyveβ-geo/β-geo mouse mutant, which expresses 10% of the wild-type levels of PIKfyve, or shRNA of PIKfyve in wild-type fibroblasts, which reduces PIKfyve to 17% of wild-type levels, each still had approximately half of the normal levels of PI3,5P2 and PI5P (Zolov et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study by Zolov et al., 2012.

claim: shRNA of PIKfyve in wild-type fibroblasts, which reduces PIKfyve to 17% of wild-type levels, resulted in approximately half of the normal levels of PI3,5P2 and PI5P.
source: In an earlier study we found that fibroblasts from a hypomorphic PIKfyveβ-geo/β-geo mouse mutant, which expresses 10% of the wild-type levels of PIKfyve, or shRNA of PIKfyve in wild-type fibroblasts, which reduces PIKfyve to 17% of wild-type levels, each still had approximately half of the normal levels of PI3,5P2 and PI5P (Zolov et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study by Zolov et al., 2012.

claim: Following 30 min of incubation in DMSO, the amount of labeled integrin at the cell border exhibited a modest decrease to 21% of total integrin.
source: Following 30 min of incubation in DMSO, the amount of labeled integrin at the cell border exhibited a modest decrease to 21% of total integrin.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from integrin trafficking experiments.

claim: Inhibition of PIKfyve for 30 min caused a decrease in the amount of integrin at the cell border to 13.7%.
source: In contrast, inhibition of PIKfyve for 30 min caused a much larger decrease in the amount of integrin at the cell border to 13.7%.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from integrin trafficking experiments.

claim: After 30 min of apilimod treatment, there was a significant increase of 0.52-fold more internalized β1-integrin compared to DMSO-treated cells.
source: Consistent with the observed changes in surface levels of integrin, we found that after 30 min of apilimod treatment, there was a significant increase of 0.52-fold more internalized β1-integrin as compared to DMSO-treated cells (Figure 2L).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from integrin internalization assays shown in Figure 2L.

claim: PIKfyve has a role in β1-integrin trafficking.
source: These results indicate that PIKfyve has a role in β1-integrin trafficking.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental results showing that PIKfyve inhibition affects β1-integrin surface levels and internalization.

claim: Endogenous 3xHA-PIKfyve exhibited the best colocalization with VPS35.
source: We observed the best colocalization with VPS35 (Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from colocalization studies shown in Figure 3.

claim: VPS35 associates with endosomes that are active in Retromer-dependent transport.
source: VPS35 associates with endosomes that are active in Retromer-dependent transport (Gallon and Cullen, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study by Gallon and Cullen, 2015.

claim: There was modest colocalization of PIKfyve with RAB7 and EEA1.
source: There was also a modest colocalization of PIKfyve with RAB7 and EEA1, and some colocalization with RAB11, LAMP1, and LAMP2.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from colocalization studies shown in Figure 3.

claim: There was some colocalization of PIKfyve with RAB11, LAMP1, and LAMP2.
source: There was also a modest colocalization of PIKfyve with RAB7 and EEA1, and some colocalization with RAB11, LAMP1, and LAMP2.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from colocalization studies shown in Figure 3.

claim: At 15 min, the amount of antibody-labeled internalized β1-integrin that recycled back to plasma membrane was significantly lowered by 0.58-fold in cells treated with apilimod compared to DMSO-treated cells.
source: Notably, at 15 min, the amount of antibody-labeled internalized β1-integrin that recycled back to plasma membrane was significantly lowered by 0.58-fold in cells treated with apilimod as compared to DMSO-treated cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from recycling assays shown in Figure 4.

claim: After 30 min of treatment, apilimod-treated cells had 0.45-fold less surface β1-integrin compared with DMSO-treated cells.
source: Moreover, after 30 min of treatment, the apilimod-treated cells had 0.45-fold less surface β1-integrin compared with DMSO-treated cells (Figure 4K).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from recycling assays shown in Figure 4K.

claim: In cells treated with apilimod for 15 min, the internal-non-recycled pool of β1-integrin was significantly higher by 20% compared with DMSO-treated cells.
source: In cells treated with apilimod for 15 min, the internal-non-recycled pool of β1-integrin was significantly higher by 20% compared with DMSO-treated cells, and this accumulation was 30% higher after 30 min of apilimod treatment (Figure 4L).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from recycling assays shown in Figure 4L.

claim: The accumulation of internal-non-recycled β1-integrin was 30% higher after 30 min of apilimod treatment compared with DMSO-treated cells.
source: In cells treated with apilimod for 15 min, the internal-non-recycled pool of β1-integrin was significantly higher by 20% compared with DMSO-treated cells, and this accumulation was 30% higher after 30 min of apilimod treatment (Figure 4L).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from recycling assays shown in Figure 4L.

claim: PIKfyve is required for the recycling of β1-integrin from internal compartments to the plasma membrane.
source: These results indicate that PIKfyve is required for the recycling of β1-integrin from internal compartments to the plasma membrane.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental results showing that PIKfyve inhibition impairs β1-integrin recycling.

claim: At 0 time, β1-integrin was predominantly present in EEA1-positive endosomes in untreated cells.
source: Consistent with previous studies, at 0 time, β1-integrin was predominantly present in EEA1-positive endosomes (untreated cells, Figure 5A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from colocalization studies shown in Figure 5A-B and is consistent with previous studies.

claim: PIKfyve inhibition resulted in significantly more labeled β1-integrin in each of the compartments that are part of its itinerary.
source: When compared with DMSO controls, PIKfyve inhibition resulted in significantly more labeled β1-integrin in each of the compartments that are part of its itinerary (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from colocalization studies shown in Figure 5B.

claim: PIKfyve activity is required for the exit of β1-integrin from several endocytic compartments.
source: This suggests that PIKfyve activity is required for the exit of β1-integrin from several endocytic compartments.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental results showing that PIKfyve inhibition causes accumulation of β1-integrin in multiple endocytic compartments.

claim: In DMSO-treated cells, the amount of integrin present in EEA1 compartments decreased by 35% at 15 min.
source: Specifically, the amount of integrin present in EEA1 compartments in DMSO-treated cells decreased by 35% at 15 min and this amount further decreased to 56% at 30 min.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from integrin trafficking experiments.

claim: In DMSO-treated cells, the amount of integrin present in EEA1 compartments decreased to 56% at 30 min.
source: Specifically, the amount of integrin present in EEA1 compartments in DMSO-treated cells decreased by 35% at 15 min and this amount further decreased to 56% at 30 min.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from integrin trafficking experiments.

claim: With PIKfyve inhibition, there was not a significant decrease in the amount of integrin present in EEA1 compartments at either 15 or 30 min.
source: In contrast, with PIKfyve inhibition, there was not a significant decrease in the amount of integrin present in EEA1 compartments at either 15 or 30 min.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from integrin trafficking experiments.

claim: PIKfyve inhibition causes a delay in the exit of integrin from early endosomes.
source: This indicates a delay in the exit of integrin from early endosomes.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental results showing that PIKfyve inhibition prevents the decrease in integrin in EEA1 compartments.

claim: In DMSO-treated cells, the amount of integrin present in LAMP1-positive compartments decreased approximately 32% at 15 and 30 min.
source: Similarly, in DMSO-treated cells, the amount of integrin present in LAMP1-positive compartments decreased approximately 32% at 15 and 30 min.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from integrin trafficking experiments.

claim: Following PIKfyve inhibition, there was no observable decrease in integrin in LAMP1 compartments.
source: However, following PIKfyve inhibition, there was no observable decrease in integrin in LAMP1 compartments.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from integrin trafficking experiments.

claim: PIKfyve inhibition causes a delay in the exit of β1-integrin from early and late endosomes.
source: Together, these data show that PIKfyve inhibition causes a delay in the exit of β1-integrin from early and late endosomes.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental results showing that PIKfyve inhibition prevents the decrease in integrin in both EEA1 and LAMP1 compartments.

claim: β1-integrin is recycled from both early and late endosomes.
source: Note that, β1-integrin is recycled from both of these compartments (Moreno-Layseca et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study by Moreno-Layseca et al., 2019.

claim: At the time points measured, PIKfyve inhibition did not impact the degradation of β1-integrin.
source: However, at the time points measured, we did not see an impact of PIKfyve inhibition on the degradation of β1-integrin.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing no change in total β1-integrin levels.

claim: The total level of β1-integrin was not significantly altered after apilimod treatment for 30 min.
source: The total level of β1-integrin was not significantly altered after apilimod treatment for 30 min (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from western blot analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: In cells treated with DMSO for 15 or 30 min, the amount of β1-integrin in RAB11-positive compartments decreased by approximately 66%.
source: In cells treated with DMSO for 15 or 30 min, the amount of β1-integrin in RAB11-positive compartments decreased by approximately 66%.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from integrin trafficking experiments.

claim: During PIKfyve inhibition, the amount of integrin in apilimod-treated cells had a more modest decrease of 22% and 34%, at 15 and 30 min of treatment, respectively.
source: In contrast, during PIKfyve inhibition the amount of integrin in apilimod-treated cells had a more modest decrease of 22% and 34%, at 15 and 30 min of treatment, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from integrin trafficking experiments.

claim: In cells treated with DMSO for 15 and 30 min, the amount of integrin remaining in RAB4 endosomes was significantly lower by 57% and 67%, respectively.
source: In cells treated with DMSO for 15 and 30 min, the amount of integrin remaining in RAB4 endosomes was significantly lower by 57% and 67%, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from integrin trafficking experiments.

claim: Following PIKfyve inhibition, the decrease in β1-integrin in RAB4 endosomes was only 27% at 15 min and 48% after 30 min.
source: In comparison, following PIKfyve inhibition, the decrease in β1-integrin in RAB4 endosomes was only 27% at 15 min and 48% after 30 min.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from integrin trafficking experiments.

claim: Short-term inhibition of PIKfyve slows the recycling of β1-integrin from RAB4 endosomes.
source: Thus, short-term inhibition of PIKfyve also slows the recycling of β1-integrin from RAB4 endosomes.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental results showing that PIKfyve inhibition reduces the rate of β1-integrin exit from RAB4 endosomes.

claim: PIKfyve plays a role in the recycling of β1-integrin from all endocytic compartments tested including early and late endosomes as well as fast and slow recycling endosomes.
source: Together, these studies suggest that PIKfyve plays a role in the recycling of β1-integrin from all endocytic compartments tested including early and late endosomes as well as fast and slow recycling endosomes.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental results showing that PIKfyve inhibition affects β1-integrin trafficking through multiple endocytic compartments.

claim: β1-integrin recycling from endosomes is regulated by the sorting nexin SNX17, the Retriever complex, the CCC complex, and the actin regulatory WASH complex.
source: β1-integrin recycling from endosomes is regulated by the sorting nexin, SNX17, the Retriever complex, the CCC complex, and the actin regulatory WASH complex (Chen et al., 2019; McNally and Cullen, 2018; Simonetti and Cullen, 2019; Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies by Chen et al., 2019; McNally and Cullen, 2018; Simonetti and Cullen, 2019; Wang et al., 2018.

claim: Loss of SNX17 inhibits the recycling of β1-integrin from endosomes.
source: Loss of SNX17 inhibits the recycling of β1-integrin from endosomes (Böttcher et al., 2012; McNally et al., 2017; Steinberg et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies by Böttcher et al., 2012; McNally et al., 2017; Steinberg et al., 2012.

claim: Inhibition of PIKfyve lowers β1-integrin levels on the cell surface by approximately 50%.
source: We performed surface biotinylation assays and found that inhibition of PIKfyve lowers β1-integrin, α5-integrin, and LRP1 levels on the cell surface by approximately 50% each (Figure 6A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from surface biotinylation assays shown in Figure 6A-B.

claim: Inhibition of PIKfyve lowers α5-integrin levels on the cell surface by approximately 50%.
source: We performed surface biotinylation assays and found that inhibition of PIKfyve lowers β1-integrin, α5-integrin, and LRP1 levels on the cell surface by approximately 50% each (Figure 6A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from surface biotinylation assays shown in Figure 6A-B.

claim: Inhibition of PIKfyve lowers LRP1 levels on the cell surface by approximately 50%.
source: We performed surface biotinylation assays and found that inhibition of PIKfyve lowers β1-integrin, α5-integrin, and LRP1 levels on the cell surface by approximately 50% each (Figure 6A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from surface biotinylation assays shown in Figure 6A-B.

claim: Depletion of PIKfyve caused a decrease in surface levels of α5-integrin by 17%.
source: Similar to PIKfyve inhibition, depletion of PIKfyve also caused a decrease in surface levels of α5-integrin levels by 17%.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from siRNA knockdown experiments shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: PIKfyve re-expression led to an increase in surface levels of α5-integrin by 47% more than the control-treated cells.
source: PIKfyve re-expression led to increase in surface levels by 47% more than the control-treated cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from rescue experiments shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: PIKfyve regulates general SNX17-Retriever-CCC-WASH-mediated recycling.
source: Together, these findings suggest that PIKfyve regulates general SNX17-Retriever-CCC-WASH-mediated recycling.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental results showing that PIKfyve inhibition affects multiple cargoes of the SNX17-Retriever-CCC-WASH pathway.

claim: Inhibition of PIKfyve does not alter the surface levels of EGFR.
source: Notably, inhibition of PIKfyve using conditions that impacted integrins and LRP1 does not alter the surface levels of EGFR (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from immunofluorescence studies shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Acute inhibition of PIKfyve does not impact all membrane trafficking pathways that require endosomal function.
source: These findings suggest that acute inhibition of PIKfyve does not impact all membrane trafficking pathways that require endosomal function.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental results showing that PIKfyve inhibition affects some receptors (integrins, LRP1) but not others (EGFR).

claim: PIKfyve colocalizes with SNX17 and subunits of the WASH (Strumpellin and FAM21), Retriever (VPS35L), and CCC (COMMD1 and CCDC93) complexes.
source: In further support that PIKfyve is required for the SNX17-Retriever-CCC-WASH pathway, we tested and found that PIKfyve colocalizes with SNX17 and subunits of the WASH (Strumpellin and FAM21), Retriever (VPS35L), and CCC (COMMD1 and CCDC93) complexes (Figure 6C–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from colocalization studies shown in Figure 6C-D.

claim: 30–50% of endogenous PIKfyve colocalizes with proteins implicated in β1-integrin recycling.
source: Utilizing Mander's coefficient, we quantified the fraction of the indicated proteins that overlap with endogenous PIKfyve-positive puncta and observed a colocalization of 30–50% of endogenous PIKfyve with the proteins implicated in β1-integrin recycling.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from colocalization quantification using Mander's coefficient.

claim: PIKfyve regulates β1-integrin recycling from endosomes via regulation of the SNX17-Retriever-CCC-WASH complex.
source: These data provide further support for the hypothesis that PIKfyve regulates β1-integrin recycling from endosomes via regulation of the SNX17-Retriever-CCC-WASH complex.
evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple experimental results showing colocalization and functional interactions between PIKfyve and the SNX17-Retriever-CCC-WASH complex.

claim: Acute inhibition of PIKfyve for 30 min caused a significant decrease in colocalization of CCC subunit COMMD1 with VPS35 endosomes by 22%.
source: Importantly, for each CCC and Retriever subunit tested, acute inhibition of PIKfyve for 30 min caused a significant decrease in their colocalization with VPS35 endosomes. The CCC subunits COMMD1, COMMD5, and CCDC93 were lowered by 22%, 20%, and 30%, respectively (Figure 7, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from colocalization studies shown in Figure 7.

claim: Acute inhibition of PIKfyve for 30 min caused a significant decrease in colocalization of CCC subunit COMMD5 with VPS35 endosomes by 20%.
source: Importantly, for each CCC and Retriever subunit tested, acute inhibition of PIKfyve for 30 min caused a significant decrease in their colocalization with VPS35 endosomes. The CCC subunits COMMD1, COMMD5, and CCDC93 were lowered by 22%, 20%, and 30%, respectively (Figure 7, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from colocalization studies shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Acute inhibition of PIKfyve for 30 min caused a significant decrease in colocalization of CCC subunit CCDC93 with VPS35 endosomes by 30%.
source: Importantly, for each CCC and Retriever subunit tested, acute inhibition of PIKfyve for 30 min caused a significant decrease in their colocalization with VPS35 endosomes. The CCC subunits COMMD1, COMMD5, and CCDC93 were lowered by 22%, 20%, and 30%, respectively (Figure 7, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from colocalization studies shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The loss of the CCC proteins from VPS35 endosomes occurred over a relatively short time frame of 30 min, which suggests that PIKfyve plays a direct role.
source: Note that the loss of the CCC proteins from VPS35 endosomes occurred over a relatively short time frame, 30 min, which suggests that PIKfyve plays a direct role.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that the effect occurs rapidly, suggesting a direct rather than indirect mechanism.

claim: siRNA depletion of PIKfyve resulted in a 15% decrease in endosomal localization of COMMD1 compared to mock siRNA-treated cells.
source: Compared to mock siRNA-treated cells, siRNA depletion of PIKfyve resulted in a 15% decrease in endosomal localization of COMMD1.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from siRNA knockdown experiments shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: The decrease in COMMD1 localization following PIKfyve depletion was rescued by expression of PIKfyve.
source: Importantly this decrease was rescued by expression of PIKfyve (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from rescue experiments shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: Some proteins in the CCC complex may directly bind PI3,5P2 and/or PI5P.
source: That the CCC subunits tested partially rely on PIKfyve for their localization suggests that some proteins in the CCC complex may directly bind PI3,5P2 and/or PI5P.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning based on the observation that CCC subunits require PIKfyve for localization.

claim: COMMD1, COMMD7, and COMMD10 bind some phosphoinositides including PI3,5P2 and in some cases PI5P in in vitro assays.
source: Notably, COMMD1, COMMD7, and COMMD10 bind some phosphoinositides including PI3,5P2 and in some cases PI5P in in vitro assays (Healy et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study by Healy et al., 2018.

claim: Acute inhibition of PIKfyve for 30 min caused a 17% decrease in the Retriever subunit VPS35L on VPS35 endosomes.
source: We also found that the Retriever subunit, VPS35L, was lowered by 17% (Figure 7A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from colocalization studies shown in Figure 7A-B.

claim: The reliance of the Retriever complex on PIKfyve may be due to direct binding of some Retriever subunits to PI3,5P2 and/or PI5P.
source: The reliance of the Retriever complex on PIKfyve may either be due to direct binding of some Retriever subunits to PI3,5P2 and/or PI5P, or may be due to a requirement for the presence of the CCC complex on endosomes, since the Retriever complex interacts with the CCC complex, and a portion of VPS35L is associated with the CCC complex (McNally et al., 2017; Phillips-Krawczak et al., 2015; Singla et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning based on the observation that Retriever requires PIKfyve and interacts with CCC, supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The reliance of the Retriever complex on PIKfyve may be due to a requirement for the presence of the CCC complex on endosomes.
source: The reliance of the Retriever complex on PIKfyve may either be due to direct binding of some Retriever subunits to PI3,5P2 and/or PI5P, or may be due to a requirement for the presence of the CCC complex on endosomes, since the Retriever complex interacts with the CCC complex, and a portion of VPS35L is associated with the CCC complex (McNally et al., 2017; Phillips-Krawczak et al., 2015; Singla et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning based on the observation that Retriever requires PIKfyve and interacts with CCC, supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Acute inhibition of PIKfyve resulted in a 27% increase in SNX17 on VPS35-positive endosomes.
source: In contrast with the partial loss of CCC and Retriever proteins from membranes, acute inhibition of PIKfyve resulted in a 27% increase in SNX17 on VPS35-positive endosomes (Figure 7A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from colocalization studies shown in Figure 7A-B.

claim: The increased recruitment of SNX17 may be due to an elevation in PI3P that occurs during inhibition of PIKfyve.
source: The increased recruitment of SNX17 may be due to an elevation in PI3P that occurs during inhibition of PIKfyve (Zolov et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning based on the observation that SNX17 increases during PIKfyve inhibition, supported by a citation to a previous study showing PI3P elevation.

claim: The WASH complex subunit FAM21 remained unchanged following acute inhibition of PIKfyve.
source: The WASH complex subunit, FAM21, remained unchanged.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from colocalization studies shown in Figure 7.

claim: In MEFs, approximately two-thirds of the PI3P pool comes from VPS34.
source: In MEFs, approximately, two-thirds of the PI3P pool comes from VPS34 (Devereaux et al., 2013; Ikonomov et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies by Devereaux et al., 2013; Ikonomov et al., 2015.

claim: Inhibition of VPS34 lowers PI3,5P2 and PI5P.
source: Note that inhibition of VPS34 also lowers PI3,5P2 and PI5P (Figure 7—figure supplement 3; Devereaux et al., 2013; Ikonomov et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3 and citations to previous studies.

claim: PI3,5P2 is synthesized from PI3P.
source: This is because PI3,5P2 is synthesized from PI3P (Sbrissa et al., 1999), and PI5P is synthesized from PI3,5P2 (Zolov et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies by Sbrissa et al., 1999.

claim: PI5P is synthesized from PI3,5P2.
source: This is because PI3,5P2 is synthesized from PI3P (Sbrissa et al., 1999), and PI5P is synthesized from PI3,5P2 (Zolov et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study by Zolov et al., 2012.

claim: Inhibition of VPS34 with VPS34-IN1 resulted in significantly less SNX17 on VPS35 endosomes.
source: To further test a role for PI3P in the recruitment of SNX17, we inhibited VPS34 with VPS34-IN1, and found that there was significantly less SNX17 on VPS35 endosomes (Figure 7—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from VPS34 inhibition studies shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 4.

claim: Inhibition of VPS34 resulted in less VPS35L and COMMD1 on VPS35 endosomes.
source: In addition, we observed less VPS35L and COMMD1.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from VPS34 inhibition studies shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 4.

claim: The decrease in VPS35L and COMMD1 following VPS34 inhibition is likely due to lower levels of PI3,5P2 and PI5P.
source: These changes are likely due to lower levels of PI3,5P2 and PI5P, as inhibition of PIKfyve with apilimod also lowered the levels of these proteins on VPS35 endosomes.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning based on the observation that both VPS34 and PIKfyve inhibition have similar effects.

claim: The levels of FAM21 were lower following VPS34 inhibition.
source: The levels of FAM21 were also lower.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from VPS34 inhibition studies shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 4.

claim: The decrease in FAM21 following VPS34 inhibition is likely due to lower levels of PI3P, PI3,5P2, and/or PI5P.
source: These changes are likely due to lower levels of the PI3P, PI3,5P2, and/or PI5P.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning based on the observation that VPS34 inhibition lowers multiple phosphoinositides.

claim: A combination of 1 μM apilimod and 0.1 µM VPS34-IN1 resulted in lower PI3,5P2 and PI5P, but normal cellular levels of PI3P.
source: To determine effects due to lowering PI3,5P2 and PI5P, under conditions where PI3P levels are not elevated, we tested and found that a combination of 1 μM apilimod, and 0.1 µM VPS34-IN1, resulted in lower PI3,5P2 and PI5P, but normal cellular levels of PI3P (Figure 7—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from phosphoinositide measurements shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 5.

claim: Lowering PI3,5P2 and PI5P under conditions without detectable changes in PI3P resulted in no change in SNX17 recruitment.
source: We tested and found that lowering PI3,5P2 and PI5P under conditions without detectable changes in PI3P resulted in no change in SNX17 recruitment.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from combined inhibitor treatment studies shown in Figure 7.

claim: Lowering PI3,5P2 and PI5P under conditions without detectable changes in PI3P resulted in less VPS35L, COMMD1, and FAM21 on VPS35 endosomes.
source: However, there was less VPS35L, COMMD1, and FAM21 on VPS35 endosomes.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from combined inhibitor treatment studies shown in Figure 7.

claim: Conversion of PI3P to PI3,5P2 or PI5P plays an important role in ordered recruitment of SNX17-Retriever-CCC-WASH complexes.
source: These studies indicate that conversion of PI3P to PI3,5P2 or PI5P plays an important role in ordered recruitment of these complexes.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental results showing differential effects of inhibiting VPS34 versus PIKfyve on complex recruitment.

claim: SNX17 requires PI3P to associate with endosomes.
source: While SNX17 requires PI3P to associate with these endosomes, VPS35L (Retriever) and COMMD1 (CCC) require the synthesis of PI3,5P2 and/or PI5P.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental results showing that SNX17 recruitment is affected by VPS34 inhibition but not by combined apilimod/VPS34-IN1 treatment.

claim: VPS35L (Retriever) and COMMD1 (CCC) require the synthesis of PI3,5P2 and/or PI5P for endosomal localization.
source: While SNX17 requires PI3P to associate with these endosomes, VPS35L (Retriever) and COMMD1 (CCC) require the synthesis of PI3,5P2 and/or PI5P.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental results showing that VPS35L and COMMD1 are affected by both PIKfyve inhibition and combined apilimod/VPS34-IN1 treatment.

claim: The localization of FAM21 to endosomes requires the generation of either PI3P, PI3,5P2, and/or PI5P.
source: Additionally, the localization of FAM21 to endosomes requires the generation of either PI3P, PI3,5P2, and/or PI5P.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental results showing that FAM21 is affected by both VPS34 and PIKfyve inhibition.

claim: FAM21 binds multiple phosphorylated phosphoinositide lipids in vitro, including PI3P.
source: Consistent with this finding, FAM21 binds multiple phosphorylated phosphoinositide lipids in vitro, including PI3P (Jia et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study by Jia et al., 2010.

claim: The SNX17-Retriever-CCC-WASH recycling pathway may be ordered by a phosphoinositide cascade.
source: Together, these findings suggest that that the SNX17-Retriever-CCC-WASH recycling pathway may be ordered by a phosphoinositide cascade, where PI3P is necessary for the recruitment of SNX17 to WASH complex-containing endosomes, and PI3P-dependent recruitment of PIKfyve generates PI3,5P2 and/or PI5P which facilitates the recruitment the CCC and Retriever complexes.
evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple experimental results showing sequential requirements for different phosphoinositides in complex recruitment.

claim: PI3P is necessary for the recruitment of SNX17 to WASH complex-containing endosomes.
source: Together, these findings suggest that that the SNX17-Retriever-CCC-WASH recycling pathway may be ordered by a phosphoinositide cascade, where PI3P is necessary for the recruitment of SNX17 to WASH complex-containing endosomes, and PI3P-dependent recruitment of PIKfyve generates PI3,5P2 and/or PI5P which facilitates the recruitment the CCC and Retriever complexes.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental results showing that SNX17 recruitment requires VPS34 activity.

claim: PI3P-dependent recruitment of PIKfyve generates PI3,5P2 and/or PI5P which facilitates the recruitment of the CCC and Retriever complexes.
source: Together, these findings suggest that that the SNX17-Retriever-CCC-WASH recycling pathway may be ordered by a phosphoinositide cascade, where PI3P is necessary for the recruitment of SNX17 to WASH complex-containing endosomes, and PI3P-dependent recruitment of PIKfyve generates PI3,5P2 and/or PI5P which facilitates the recruitment the CCC and Retriever complexes.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental results showing that CCC and Retriever recruitment requires PIKfyve activity.

claim: Mutation of residues R133, H134, and K167 in COMMD1 to R133Q, H134A, and K167A (COMMD1-QAA) abolished the ability of COMMD1 to bind phosphoinositide lipids in vitro.
source: Mutation of residues that comprise a basic patch on COMMD1, R133Q, H134A, and K167A (COMMD1-QAA) abolished the ability of COMMD1 to bind phosphoinositide lipids in vitro (Healy et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study by Healy et al., 2018.

claim: The COMMD1-QAA mutant binds membranes in cells.
source: However, this mutant bounds membranes in cells, although there were no further tests of function.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study by Healy et al., 2018.

claim: There was no statistically significant difference in the binding of COMMD1 and the COMMD1-QAA mutant to endosomes.
source: We expressed this mutant as well as the original COMMD1-QAA mutant in COMMD1-/- cells and found that as previously reported, there was no statistically significant difference in the binding of COMMD1 and the original COMMD1-QAA mutant to endosomes, 17.1% and 15.9%, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from membrane binding assays shown in Figure 8.

claim: The COMMD1-EQE mutant exhibited a statistically significant defect in its association with VPS35 endosomes, where 14.8% bound.
source: In contrast, the COMMD1-EQE mutant exhibited a statistically significant defect in its association with VPS35 endosomes, where 14.8% bound (Figure 8B–C, Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from membrane binding assays shown in Figure 8B-C.

claim: The phosphoinositide binding site of COMMD1 contributes to its association with membranes.
source: These findings suggest that the phosphoinositide binding site of COMMD1 contributes to its association with membranes.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental results showing that the COMMD1-EQE mutant has reduced membrane binding.

claim: Cells expressing wild-type COMMD1 or COMMD1-QAA mutant exhibited a partial rescue of the recycling defect observed in non-transfected COMMD1-/- cells, and retained 23% less non-recycled β1-integrin compared to untransfected cells.
source: Cells expressing either wild-type COMMD1 or COMMD1-QAA mutant exhibited a partial rescue of the recycling defect observed in non-transfected COMMD1-/- cells, and retained 23% less non-recycled β1-integrin compared to untransfected cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from β1-integrin recycling assays shown in Figure 9.

claim: The COMMD1-EQE mutant failed to rescue the recycling defect in COMMD1-/- cells.
source: Importantly, the COMMD-EQE mutant failed to rescue the recycling defect.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from β1-integrin recycling assays shown in Figure 9.

claim: Cells expressing the COMMD1-EQE mutant retained 36.2% more integrin than cells rescued with COMMD1 or COMMD1-QAA.
source: Cells expressing the COMMD1-EQE mutant retained 36.2% more integrin than cells rescued with COMMD1 or COMMD1-QAA, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from β1-integrin recycling assays shown in Figure 9.

claim: The COMMD1-QAA mutant was expressed at 8.6-fold higher levels than wild-type COMMD1.
source: Surprisingly, we found that the COMMD1-QAA mutant was expressed at 8.6-fold higher levels than wild-type COMMD1.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from western blot analysis shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mutation of R133, H134, and K167 in COMMD1 partially affected the binding between CCDC93 and COMMD1.
source: However, we tested and found that mutation of these sites also resulted in a partial defect in COMMD1 association with the CCC subunit, CCDC93.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from co-immunoprecipitation assays shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: Both the COMMD1-QAA and COMMD1-EQE mutant had 40% and 60% less association with CCDC93, respectively, when compared with wild-type COMMD1.
source: When accounting for the amount of COMMD1 pulled down in each experiment, both the COMMD1-QAA and COMMD1-EQE mutant had 40% and 60% less association with CCDC93, when compared with wild-type COMMD1.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from co-immunoprecipitation assays shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: Apilimod or siRNA depletion of PIKfyve impairs the SNX17 recycling pathway.
source: Importantly, the experiments showing that apilimod or siRNA depletion of PIKfyve impairs the SNX17 recycling pathway, and results in a loss of the CCC complex and Retriever complex from endosomes, suggests that PI3,5P2 and PI5P play important roles in regulating the recruitment and/or function some CCC and possibly some Retriever subunits.
evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple experimental results showing that PIKfyve inhibition or depletion affects the SNX17 pathway and complex localization.

claim: PI3,5P2 and PI5P play important roles in regulating the recruitment and/or function of some CCC and possibly some Retriever subunits.
source: Importantly, the experiments showing that apilimod or siRNA depletion of PIKfyve impairs the SNX17 recycling pathway, and results in a loss of the CCC complex and Retriever complex from endosomes, suggests that PI3,5P2 and PI5P play important roles in regulating the recruitment and/or function some CCC and possibly some Retriever subunits.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental results showing that PIKfyve products are required for CCC and Retriever localization.

claim: PIKfyve negatively regulates cortactin, which in turn causes excessive Arp2/3 activity and hyperaccumulation of actin on endosomes.
source: A previous study revealed that PIKfyve negatively regulates cortactin, which in turn causes excessive Arp2/3 activity and hyperaccumulation of actin on endosomes (Hong et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study by Hong et al., 2015.

claim: In the shorter time frame of PIKfyve inhibition used in this study, there were no changes in the amount of cortactin that localizes to endosomes.
source: However, in the shorter time frame of PIKfyve inhibition used in this study, we did not find any changes in the amount of cortactin that localizes to endosomes (Figure 7—figure supplement 8).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from cortactin localization studies shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 8.

claim: Inhibition or depletion of PIKfyve results in enlarged lysosomes and late endosomes.
source: Inhibition or depletion of PIKfyve results in enlarged lysosomes and late endosomes (de Araujo et al., 2020; Dove et al., 2009; Ho et al., 2012; McCartney et al., 2014a; Shisheva, 2012), and indeed, PIKfyve regulates multiple pathways that contribute to lysosome function.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies by de Araujo et al., 2020; Dove et al., 2009; Ho et al., 2012; McCartney et al., 2014a; Shisheva, 2012.

claim: PIKfyve regulates multiple lysosomal ion channels.
source: These include the regulation of multiple lysosomal ion channels (Chen et al., 2017; Dong et al., 2010; Fine et al., 2018; She et al., 2018; She et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2017), as well as roles in the fission and reformation of lysosomes and related organelles (Bissig et al., 2017; Choy et al., 2018; Krishna et al., 2016; Yordanov et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies by Chen et al., 2017; Dong et al., 2010; Fine et al., 2018; She et al., 2018; She et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2017.

claim: PIKfyve plays roles in the fission and reformation of lysosomes and related organelles.
source: These include the regulation of multiple lysosomal ion channels (Chen et al., 2017; Dong et al., 2010; Fine et al., 2018; She et al., 2018; She et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2017), as well as roles in the fission and reformation of lysosomes and related organelles (Bissig et al., 2017; Choy et al., 2018; Krishna et al., 2016; Yordanov et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies by Bissig et al., 2017; Choy et al., 2018; Krishna et al., 2016; Yordanov et al., 2019.

claim: PIKfyve has roles at endosomes and has a direct role in the regulation of the SNX17-Retriever-CCC-WASH complex.
source: The studies reported here reveal that PIKfyve has roles at endosomes and has a direct role in the regulation of the SNX17-Retriever-CCC-WASH complex.
evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple experimental results showing PIKfyve localization to endosomes and its effects on the SNX17-Retriever-CCC-WASH complex.

claim: Endogenously tagged PIKfyve extensively colocalizes with SNX17, Retriever, CCC, and WASH complexes.
source: Moreover, endogenously tagged PIKfyve extensively colocalizes with SNX17, Retriever, CCC, and WASH complexes.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from colocalization studies shown in Figure 6.

claim: PIKfyve has a robust 44% colocalization with VPS35, a subunit of the Retromer complex.
source: PIKfyve has a robust 44% colocalization with VPS35, a subunit of the Retromer complex, as well as with the Retriever subunit, VPS35L.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from colocalization studies shown in Figure 3.

claim: A major pool of PIKfyve is localized to endosomal compartments involved in recycling.
source: Thus, the hypothesis that a major pool of PIKfyve is localized to endosomal compartments involved in recycling fits with the observation that the best colocalization of PIKfyve is with VPS35, followed by good colocalization with EEA1 and RAB7.
evidence: The claim is inferred from colocalization data showing PIKfyve association with markers of recycling endosomes.

claim: Activation of PIKfyve had the opposite effect of PIKfyve inhibition on β1-integrin recycling.
source: Importantly, activation of PIKfyve had the opposite effect of PIKfyve inhibition, which provides additional evidence that PI3,5P2 and/or PI5P play direct roles in the SNX17-Retriever-CCC-WASH pathway, and in β1-integrin recycling.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing that hyperactive PIKfyve increases β1-integrin surface levels.

claim: PI3,5P2 and/or PI5P play direct roles in the SNX17-Retriever-CCC-WASH pathway.
source: Importantly, activation of PIKfyve had the opposite effect of PIKfyve inhibition, which provides additional evidence that PI3,5P2 and/or PI5P play direct roles in the SNX17-Retriever-CCC-WASH pathway, and in β1-integrin recycling.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental results showing that both inhibition and activation of PIKfyve affect the pathway in opposite directions.

claim: VPS34 provides the PI3P for recruitment of SNX17.
source: VPS34, which resides on endosomes (Christoforidis et al., 1999), provides the PI3P (Figure 7, Figure 7—figure supplement 1) for recruitment of SNX17 (Chandra et al., 2019; Jia et al., 2014), where it can then bind its cargoes (Böttcher et al., 2012; Steinberg et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and citations to previous studies showing VPS34 generates PI3P that recruits SNX17.

claim: The generation of PI3P recruits PIKfyve via its FYVE domain.
source: The generation of PI3P also recruits PIKfyve, via its FYVE domain (Stenmark et al., 2002), which initiates the production of PI3,5P2 and PI5P.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study by Stenmark et al., 2002.

claim: PI3P, or PI3,5P2 and PI5P play a role in the endosomal localization of the WASH complex.
source: Note that PI3P, or PI3,5P2 and PI5P also play a role in the endosomal localization of the WASH complex (Jia et al., 2010) (and Figure 7, Figure 7—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7 and a citation to a previous study by Jia et al., 2010.

claim: The endosomal association of the WASH complex requires the Retromer complex.
source: The endosomal association of the WASH complex also requires the Retromer complex (Harbour et al., 2010; Harbour et al., 2012; Helfer et al., 2013; Jia et al., 2012; Zavodszky et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies by Harbour et al., 2010; Harbour et al., 2012; Helfer et al., 2013; Jia et al., 2012; Zavodszky et al., 2014.

claim: The generation of PI3,5P2 and/or PI5P facilitates the recruitment of the CCC complex.
source: The generation of PI3,5P2 and/or PI5P then facilitates the recruitment of the CCC complex (Figure 7).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: The CCC complex binds the WASH complex via direct interaction of CCDC93 with the WASH subunit FAM21.
source: The CCC complex also binds the WASH complex via direct interaction of CCDC93 with the WASH subunit, FAM21 (Phillips-Krawczak et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study by Phillips-Krawczak et al., 2015.

claim: The Retriever complex may associate with endosomes via directly binding to PI3,5P2 and/or PI5P.
source: The Retriever complex may associate with endosomes via directly binding to PI3,5P2 and/or PI5P (Figure 7), and/or may indirectly require PIKfyve activity to recruit and/or stabilize the CCC complex.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning based on experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: The Retriever complex may indirectly require PIKfyve activity to recruit and/or stabilize the CCC complex.
source: The Retriever complex may associate with endosomes via directly binding to PI3,5P2 and/or PI5P (Figure 7), and/or may indirectly require PIKfyve activity to recruit and/or stabilize the CCC complex.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning based on the observation that Retriever interacts with CCC.

claim: The Retriever complex interacts with and requires the CCC complex to bind to endosomes.
source: Note that the Retriever complex interacts with and requires the CCC complex to bind to endosomes (McNally et al., 2017; Phillips-Krawczak et al., 2015; Singla et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies by McNally et al., 2017; Phillips-Krawczak et al., 2015; Singla et al., 2019.

claim: The Retriever subunit VPS26C interacts directly with SNX17.
source: In addition, the Retriever subunit, VPS26C, interacts directly with SNX17 (Farfán et al., 2013; McNally et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies by Farfán et al., 2013; McNally et al., 2017.

claim: SNX17 and the WASH complex can bind to endosomes without the Retriever and CCC complexes.
source: The studies reported here also show that SNX17 and the WASH complex can bind to endosomes without the Retriever and CCC complexes.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing that SNX17 and WASH remain on endosomes during PIKfyve inhibition while Retriever and CCC are lost.

claim: Endosomes that contain SNX17 and the WASH complex are not sufficient for the recruitment of either the Retriever or CCC complexes.
source: However, endosomes that contain SNX17 and the WASH complex are not sufficient for the recruitment of either the Retriever or CCC complexes.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental results showing that PIKfyve activity is required for Retriever and CCC recruitment even when SNX17 and WASH are present.

claim: PIKfyve activity is needed for recruitment of Retriever and CCC complexes.
source: PIKfyve activity is also needed for recruitment of Retriever and CCC complexes.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing that PIKfyve inhibition causes loss of Retriever and CCC from endosomes.

claim: The CCC subunit CCDC22 recruits MTMR2, which is required for late steps in the SNX17-Retriever-CCC-WASH recycling pathway.
source: Furthermore, the CCC subunit CCDC22 recruits MTMR2, which is required for late steps in this recycling pathway (Singla et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study by Singla et al., 2019.

claim: Recruitment of MTMR2 lowers PI3P and PI3,5P2.
source: Importantly, we found that recruitment of MTMR2 lowers both PI3P and PI3,5P2 (Singla et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study by Singla et al., 2019.

claim: The SNX17-Retriever-CCC-WASH pathway may be ordered in part via an initiation step that involves PI3P, middle steps that require PI3,5P2 and/or PI5P and a late step via MTMR2 that removes PI3P and PI3,5P2.
source: Thus, the SNX17-Retriever-CCC-WASH pathway may be ordered in part via an initiation step that involves PI3P, middle steps that require PI3,5P2 and/or PI5P and a late step via MTMR2 that removes PI3P and PI3,5P2.
evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple experimental results showing sequential requirements for different phosphoinositides and MTMR2 action.

claim: Once the SNX17-Retriever-CCC-WASH complex assembles with cargo, the WASH complex mediates actin nucleation.
source: Finally, once the SNX17-Retriever-CCC-WASH complex assembles with cargo, the WASH complex mediates actin nucleation (Derivery et al., 2009; Gomez and Billadeau, 2009) and SNX17 recruits EHD1 (Dhawan et al., 2020) to enable fission of cargo containing membrane for efficient recycling.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies by Derivery et al., 2009; Gomez and Billadeau, 2009.

claim: SNX17 recruits EHD1 to enable fission of cargo containing membrane for efficient recycling.
source: Finally, once the SNX17-Retriever-CCC-WASH complex assembles with cargo, the WASH complex mediates actin nucleation (Derivery et al., 2009; Gomez and Billadeau, 2009) and SNX17 recruits EHD1 (Dhawan et al., 2020) to enable fission of cargo containing membrane for efficient recycling.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study by Dhawan et al., 2020.

claim: Positive regulation of the SNX17-Retriever-CCC-WASH pathway may occur via direct binding of some of the subunits within these complexes to PI3P and PI3,5P2 or PI5P.
source: While we favor a model where positive regulation of the SNX17-Retriever-CCC-WASH pathway occurs via direct binding of some of the subunits within these complexes to PI3P and PI3,5P2 or PI5P, it is possible that these lipids are impacting the pathway in a more global way.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning based on experimental results showing phosphoinositide requirements for complex recruitment.

claim: PIKfyve is important for endosome maturation.
source: For example, PIKfyve is important for endosome maturation (Kim et al., 2014; Messenger et al., 2015), and this could play a role in how PIKfyve regulates the SNX17-Retriever-CCC-WASH pathway.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies by Kim et al., 2014; Messenger et al., 2015.

claim: Treatment of cells with 100 nM apilimod for 16 hr resulted in a reduction in steady-state levels of exogenously expressed FLAG-TGFβ-R2 at the cell surface.
source: The new role for PIKfyve in endocytic recycling reported here may partially explain a recent study which showed that treatment of cells with 100 nM apilimod for 16 hr resulted in a reduction in steady-state levels of exogenously expressed, FLAG-TGFβ-R2 at the cell surface.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study by Cinato et al., 2021.

claim: The PIKfyve pathway plays a role in the formation of Stage I melanosomes, which are derived from early endosomes.
source: Previous studies have also revealed roles for PIKfyve on endosomes. The PIKfyve pathway plays a role in the formation of Stage I melanosomes, which are derived from early endosomes (Bissig et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study by Bissig et al., 2019.

claim: Knock-down of the PIKfyve pathway causes a defect in recycling of CI-MPR from endosomes to the trans-Golgi network.
source: Furthermore, we and others previously showed that knock-down of the PIKfyve pathway causes a defect in recycling of CI-MPR from endosomes to the trans-Golgi network (de Lartigue et al., 2009; Rutherford et al., 2006; Zhang et al., 2007), although the mechanistic basis of this defect remains unknown.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies by de Lartigue et al., 2009; Rutherford et al., 2006; Zhang et al., 2007.

claim: SNX11 binds to PI3,5P2.
source: Moreover, a recent study revealed that SNX11, which plays a role in the delivery of some cargoes from endosomes to lysosomes, binds to PI3,5P2 (Xu et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study by Xu et al., 2020.

claim: PIKfyve inhibition caused the accumulation of the tight junction proteins claudin1 and claudin2 into endosomes and delayed the formation of epithelial permeability barrier.
source: In addition, PIKfyve inhibition caused the accumulation of the tight junction proteins, claudin1 and claudin2, into endosomes and delayed the formation of epithelial permeability barrier (Dukes et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study by Dukes et al., 2012.

claim: PIKfyve inhibition did not affect the surface localization of claudin4.
source: Interestingly, PIKfyve inhibition did not affect the surface localization of claudin4 or the surface levels of EGFR (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study by Dukes et al., 2012.

claim: PIKfyve regulates specific recycling pathways.
source: This suggests that PIKfyve regulates specific recycling pathways.
evidence: The claim is inferred from observations that PIKfyve inhibition affects some receptors but not others.

claim: Heterologous studies in Xenopus laevis oocytes suggested a connection between PIKfyve activity and RAB11 endosomes that regulate endocytic recycling.
source: Additionally, heterologous studies in Xenopus laevis oocytes suggested a connection between PIKfyve activity and RAB11 endosomes that regulate endocytic recycling (Seebohm et al., 2012; Seebohm et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies by Seebohm et al., 2012; Seebohm et al., 2007.

claim: PIKfyve provides acute regulation of the levels of the α-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid receptor (AMPAR) at neuronal postsynaptic sites.
source: Furthermore, we previously found that PIKfyve provides acute regulation of the levels of the α-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid receptor (AMPAR) at neuronal postsynaptic sites (McCartney et al., 2014b; Zhang et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies by McCartney et al., 2014b; Zhang et al., 2012.

claim: PIKfyve is a negative regulator of AMPAR recycling.
source: Those studies suggested that PIKfyve is a negative regulator of AMPAR recycling, which is the opposite of PIKfyve providing positive regulation of α5-integrin, β1-integrin, and LRP1 recycling.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies by McCartney et al., 2014b; Zhang et al., 2012.

claim: AMPAR recycles via the SNX27-Retromer pathway.
source: The difference may be that while these latter proteins traffic via the SNX17-Retriever-CCC-WASH pathway, AMPAR recycles via the SNX27-Retromer pathway (Hussain et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study by Hussain et al., 2014.

claim: PIKfyve may also regulate cell migration via the activation of the Rac1-GTPase.
source: In addition to regulating surface levels of β1-integrin, PIKfyve likely regulates cell migration via control of additional pathways. Previous studies suggested that PIKfyve may also regulate cell migration via the activation of the Rac1-GTPase (Dayam et al., 2017; Oppelt et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies by Dayam et al., 2017; Oppelt et al., 2014.

claim: There is extensive cross-talk between Rho GTPases and focal adhesions.
source: In addition, there is extensive cross-talk between Rho GTPases and focal adhesions (Vitali et al., 2019), thus integrin trafficking and Rac1 activation may be linked with each other.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study by Vitali et al., 2019.

claim: Apilimod has been proposed as a drug to investigate further for the treatment of COVID-19.
source: Apilimod, the PIKfyve inhibitor used in these studies, has recently been proposed as a drug to investigate further for the treatment of COVID-19 (Kang et al., 2020; Ou et al., 2020; Riva et al., 2020), and also blocks the infection of Ebola virus in cells (Nelson et al., 2017; Qiu et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies by Kang et al., 2020; Ou et al., 2020; Riva et al., 2020.

claim: Apilimod blocks the infection of Ebola virus in cells.
source: Apilimod, the PIKfyve inhibitor used in these studies, has recently been proposed as a drug to investigate further for the treatment of COVID-19 (Kang et al., 2020; Ou et al., 2020; Riva et al., 2020), and also blocks the infection of Ebola virus in cells (Nelson et al., 2017; Qiu et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies by Nelson et al., 2017; Qiu et al., 2018.

claim: Apilimod may block SARS-CoV-2 entry via loss of positive regulation of TPC2.
source: Apilimod may block SARS-CoV-2 entry via loss of positive regulation of TPC2, a downstream target of PIKfyve that resides on lysosomes (Ou et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study by Ou et al., 2020.

claim: ACE2 and Neuropilin-1 have been proposed to serve as receptors for SARS-CoV-2.
source: ACE2 and Neuropilin-1 levels at the plasma membrane are regulated. Importantly, each have been proposed to serve as receptors for SARS-CoV-2 (Daly et al., 2020; Wrapp et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies by Daly et al., 2020; Wrapp et al., 2020.

claim: A genome-wide screen identified subunits of the CCC, Retriever, and WASH complexes as proteins that regulate entry of SARS-CoV2.
source: Moreover, a genome-wide screen to identify proteins that regulate entry of SARS-CoV2 identified subunits of the CCC, Retriever, and WASH complexes (Zhu et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study by Zhu et al., 2021.
